speechtext:

Considering that Air Canada aircraft operate at less than 60 per cent of capacity and that in some areas aircraft are the only means of transportation available; considering that there are about three million people in Canada who are 60 or over and that many would fly more often if travel rates were lower; considering that only private carriers such as Quebecair and Nordair offer reduced rates of some 50 per cent for senior citizens along with the privilege of making reservations at any time, while Air Canada's reduced rates do not vary more than 9 per cent or 10 per cent, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with an important matter.
As the government is due to announce its new dairy policy next April, as the dairy producers have found themselves in a dramatic situation for a number of years and as their problems are growing, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise):
That this House unanimously urge the responsible minister to incorporate in his new policy the following recommendations: (1) That the government adopt a dairy policy applicable for five years; (2) That the Canadian Dairy Commission be granted the same authority and prerogatives as the Canadian Wheat Board; (3) That price indexing apply to dairy production as soon as prices fluctuate by 2 per cent, either way; (4) That imports of cheese be reduced to 15 million pounds; (5) That the new quota calendar be changed to lessen its seasonal character.
Those, then, are the few recommendations that must be included in the new dairy policy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. From what sources is the minister getting his primary economic advice these days? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On January 30, in reply to a question of mine concerning the cost of recovery of the Russian satellite, the Minister of National Defence replied, in part, "the international regime will meet its

responsibilities as was indicated to the Department of External Affairs by the Soviet ambassador". Does that mean Russia has given us formal assurances that it will pay all search and recovery costs and, if not, what does that remark mean?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DISINTEGRATION OF SOVIET SATELLITE OVER CANADIAN SOIL-LIABILITY FOR SEARCH AND RECOVERY COSTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not in the House when that remark was made. I would like to look at it in detail. I can tell the hon. member in general terms, of course, that yesterday-I believe he is familiar with this fact-I tabled in the House notes which we had sent to the Soviet embassy as well as to the Secretary General of the United Nations. Each one of these notes was designed to establish the fact that we were now satisfied that the debris was, in fact, part of the Soviet satellite.
This was an initial, and necessary, first step under international rules in order to lay the groundwork for a possible claim. So far-I believe the hon. member is also aware of this-the Soviets have not acknowledged specifically that the debris found in Canada is, indeed, part of their satellite. There will have to be an acknowledgement, first of all, on their part before the next phase can take place.

subtopic: DISINTEGRATION OF SOVIET SATELLITE OVER CANADIAN SOIL-LIABILITY FOR SEARCH AND RECOVERY COSTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and only yesterday, at long last, 1 read the note which he sent to Russia. This note was sent in accordance with article V, paragraph 1, of the treaty. It is now obvious that we have not recovered the core of the nuclear reactor. Can the minister give us any assurance that Russia will not claim that our failure to request assistance under paragraph 4 extended unduly the time and cost of recovery operations? In other words, I suggest that if the U.S.S.R. looks at the list of recovered items and decides they are worthless, we will be stuck with meeting the entire cost of the search and recovery operations.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DISINTEGRATION OF SOVIET SATELLITE OVER CANADIAN SOIL-LIABILITY FOR SEARCH AND RECOVERY COSTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the latter part of the question is, of course, a conclusion to which I can neither agree nor disagree at the moment, not having heard from the Soviets. But 1 repeat, that I believe we have taken all the steps which we can take at this particular time, and we have taken the necessary first step. These were to indicate to the Soviet Union, unmistakably, that we believe the debris concerned in this case belongs to the Soviet satellite. The next steps will be through the United Nations mechanisms to which the hon. member made reference. I am going to the United Nations tomorrow and I am sure 1 will have an opportunity to discuss this matter with Mr. Waldheim on the weekend and to clarify more fully what procedures should be followed from this point.

Mr. Speaker, at noon today, on my instructions, the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs requested the Ambassador of the Soviet Union to withdraw 11 Soviet nationals from Canada for engaging in inadmissible activities in violation of the Official Secrets Act, and of course of their status in Canada. Two other Soviet nationals who were involved have already departed Canada but will not be permitted to return. A strong protest has been conveyed to the Soviet authorities about these activities.
The Soviet Ambassador was informed that the Canadian government had irrefutable evidence that all 13 persons had been involved in an attempt to recruit a member of the RCMP in order to penetrate the RCMP Security Service. Nine of the Soviet nationals still in Canada are employees of the Soviet embassy, one is an official of the Soviet Trade Office in Ottawa, and one is a member of the International Civil Aviation Organization Secretariat in Montreal.

The Canadian authorities have informed the Ambassador of the Soviet Union today of the discovery of an attempt by the


Espionage
Soviet intelligence service to recruit a member of the RCMP in order to penetrate the RCMP Security Service. Thirteen nationals of the Soviet Union have been involved in this operation. Two have already left Canada and the eleven others have been requested to do so. Nine are employees of the Soviet Embassy in Ottawa; one is an employee of the Secretariat of the International Civil Aviation Organization in Montreal and one is an official of the Soviet Trade Office in Ottawa.
Not only did this operation involve a large number of persons but it had been elaborately planned, involving coded messages, clandestine meetings, secret concealment devices and the payment of $30,500. This unsuccessful operation was mounted by the Soviet intelligence service in April, 1977. It has involved no compromise to national security.

The Soviet nationals involved are:
Igor P. Vartanian, First Secretary responsible for sports and cultural affairs, Soviet embassy, Ottawa.
Nikolai M. Talanov, counsellor, Soviet embassy, Ottawa.
Anatoly A. Mikhalin, official of the Soviet Foreign Trade Office, Ottawa.
Vadim A. Borishpolets, attache (Consular Affairs), Soviet embassy, Ottawa.
Vladimir L. Souvorov, Second Secretary, Soviet embassy, Ottawa.
Vladimir I. Oshkaderov, translator, International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), Montreal.
Yevgeniy K. Koblov, clerk, Soviet embassy, Ottawa.
Gennadi V. Ivashavitch, Third Secretary, Soviet embassy, Ottawa.
Oleg D. Reztsov, attache, Soviet embassy, Ottawa.
Vera A. Reztsov, employed in the library of the Soviet embassy, Ottawa.
Petr R. Lillenurm, Second Secretary (Consular Affairs), Soviet embassy, Ottawa.
Voldemar P. Veber, formerly Second Secretary in the Consular Division, Soviet embassy, Ottawa. Returned to the U.S.S.R. July 1977.
Andrei V. Krysin, economist, Soviet Foreign Trade Office, Ottawa. Returned to the U.S.S.R. December 1977.
Early in 1977 two Soviet intelligence officers approached a member of the RCMP and offered him an unlimited sum of money to spy for them. This member of the force had, on an earlier posting and in the normal course of his responsibilities, come into infrequent contact with one of the Soviet officials in this case. To establish the ultimate purpose of the Soviet approach, the member of the force was authorized, by the RCMP, under carefully controlled circumstances, to meet with the principal agent, Mr. Vartanian, in accordance with elaborate instructions he had received from the two Soviet officials. Between April, 1977, and the present he met secretly with the principal agent on seven occasions.

The 12 other Soviet nationals identified with this operation were involved in different support functions including transportation, counter-surveillance, and regular weekly observation activities.
This case proved to be a classic example of an intelligence operation, involving complex signalling systems, coded passwords, and secret concealment devices, all for the purpose of arranging clandestine meetings between the RCMP member and the Soviet agent.
As an example, on different occasions filmed instructions were passed to the RCMP member in a hollowed-out stick and a specially prepared package of cigarettes. The RCMP member was instructed by the agent to obtain information on such subjects as the methods the RCMP Security Service employed against Soviet intelligence services in Canada, character assessments of RCMP personnel, and details regarding RCMP counter-espionage cases. The RCMP member in return provided the Soviets with carefully screened non-sensitive information or completely fabricated material. The fact that he was paid $30,500 for information of no consequence provides an indication of the importance the Soviet intelligence service attached to this operation. The important point for the House to note, however, is that this case has involved no compromise of Canada's security.
This Soviet recruitment attempt is, nevertheless, a source of serious concern to the government. Its importance should be seen in the context of the unusual lengths to which the Soviet intelligence service was prepared to go to suborn a member of the RCMP. The case did not have any other implications for Canada's security. The evidence derived from this operation indicates that it was directed solely against the RCMP.
The firm action taken by the government in this case will remind the Soviet Union of our determination to deter foreign espionage. The government regrets that activities of this kind should be conducted at a time when there are efforts under way, to which both Canada and the Soviet Union have subscribed, to reduce the level of international tensions by overcoming mistrust and increasing confidence. Activities such as those I have disclosed to the House are contrary to that objective and represent a serious setback in our bilateral relations. This incident, and the action we have had to take today, will inevitably place strains on our relations with the Soviet Union. Nevertheless the Canadian government continues to attach importance to Canadian-Soviet relations and hopes the Soviet government does likewise.

There can be no doubt that this represents a serious setback, clearly in the face of those people of good will in both governments who, in recent years, have been attempting to improve and make more civilized the relationships between our two peoples. The authorities in the Soviet Union, who are responsible for these despicable activities, now have to assume responsibility for the unfortunate consequences which will follow from them.
It is worth emphasizing the Soviet Union, although it would be naive to ignore other great powers in the world which are still conducting these kinds of activities. But in this particular instance we are discussing the Soviet Union. The fact that this is still ongoing in 1978-and we are not back in the forties or fifties-indeed clearly illustrates how far we have yet to go in the modern world in trying to establish civilized and decent working relationships among all the nation states.
Under the circumstances, the response of the government in requesting the expulsion of 11 Soviet nationals who are still here, and the retention at home of two others who went back to the Soviet Union for a vist and planned to return, is entirely acceptable. Is this sufficient in terms of the relationships which were improving between Canada and the U.S.S.R.? We saw the clear possibility of the expansion of trade and the expansion of intercourse between our peoples, and now we witness this kind of dastardly act inflicted upon us. I raise the question as to the appropriateness of the government's response. In the view of my colleagues, certainly the minimum is to request those who were at fault to stay out of our country. However, on behalf of my colleagues, it seems to me something else should be done. I suggest, with all seriousness, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should think about the appropriateness of withdrawing the Canadian ambassador from Moscow on a temporary basis until relationships, and particularly this incident, are clearly discused and resolved.

We do not often have the opportunity to agree to discuss a matter as serious as that which has just been brought up in the House of Commons by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As a Canadian, I was shocked to learn that Soviet citizens employed in the U.S.S.R. embassy in Canada had taken part in espionage activities. It seems to me that this can be explained in wartime as it is then more or less normal for countries to try to learn the secrets of others. But in peacetime, and I hope that we are now in peacetime, when we try to work together to improve relations among nations so that peace may bring about more prosperity in each country, such situations are truly shocking.
Mr. Speaker, 1 am convinced that today in the House, certain members have related the important matter communicated to us by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Igor Gouzenko espionage affair which happened a few years ago and which received much publicity. I recall this affair very well and I would like the younger members of the House to take the trouble to get to the bottom of things before relating this espionage activity of a few years ago and that of which we have just been informed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Mr. Speaker, I also recall that on December 20 of last year, there was a debate in parliament about external affairs. I remember very well that all hon. members who took part in this debate showed much patriotic feeling and supported the external policy of our country. Whatever the party in power, as I said at that time, Canada is a country whose citizens are respected and loved throughout the world.
I also remember, I think it was in October 1973 if my memory serves me right, that I had the honour to participate in a NATO conference in Turkey. It was on the U.S.S.R. border. At that time aircraft were flying over an their way to Lebanon where the war was going on. I was very upset to hear the noise of those heavy aircraft transporting armaments and soldiers going to a foreign country. At that time, Mr. Speaker, you were also a member of the delegation and you participated in a debate of the NATO Plenary Assembly and I remember very well what you said. In fact you expressed the hope as a member of that delegation that as long as Canada is a democracy it will promote that detente between the two blocks. I still agree today that we should do everything to encourage the detente. As Canadians, we have, more than anyone else, an interest in encouraging that detente as geographically we are between two great nations with incredible strength. On one side the U.S.S.R. and on the other the United States.


We must be very careful every day that the little secrets we have to ensure our defence are not known by those big powers so that we can ensure our independence and security. If we always act as we did today by making the whole population aware of the dangers of spying activities within our borders we shall draw the problem to the attention of every Canadian so that every one, whatever his language or religion, will be first of all a Canadian proud of his country and ready to defend it against everyone, and ready to co-operate with the government to ensure the security of our country and make sure that in foreign embassies on Canadian territory no one is working to discover our little secrets, of which we are proud, but rather to establish better co-operation within our nation through those embassies.
Once more I commend the Secretary of State for External Affairs and I wish him good health so that he can achieve his mission. I saw him last week on TV like other hon. members when he was travelling in China to meet the great leaders of that country. Notwithstanding our political views and options, when international matters and relationships with other nations are at stake we must all share the same pride in our country and defend our Canadian rights throughout the world.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 have a number of very important questions, so I hope Your Honour will bear with me. Some of the speakers today indicated shock at what has happened in this regard. I am not shocked or surprised whatsoever because, as the minister will recall, well over a year ago I made public a list of individuals whom I asked the government to inquire into. Individuals from inside the Soviet embassy were involved, I thought, in activities incompatible with their status as diplomats. I have not double checked, but at least eight or nine people on the list to which I have just referred have either already been asked to leave the country or have now been expelled, including the principal agent, Mr. Vartanian. Since some of these so-called diplomats have been asked to leave the country, what assurance does the minister have that the government has cleaned house, and why has it taken so long since I made this list public to bring this matter forward?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXPULSION OF SOVIET UNION DIPLOMATS AND EMBASSY
subsubtopic: EMPLOYEES-ATTEMPT TO BREACH NATIONAL SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, not meaning any offence to the hon. member, I am sure he would accept that if he was in possession of that list, the RCMP and perhaps some others were in possession of it as well. The mere fact that the association of a resident diplomat with the KGB or, for that matter, any other foreign intelligence agency, is known is not of itself, obviously, sufficient evidence on which to take either expulsive action or anything related to it. What is necessary is to establish that the conduct of that person is inconsistent with his status in Canada as a registered diplomat. I think it has been said by hon. members on both sides of the House that the RCMP was aware of the list to which the hon. member referred, has been very diligent, and has produced over a period of approximately seven months evidence which is adequate to take the actions we have taken today.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister indicated that nine embassy employees and four others, a total of 13, were involved in recruiting the RCMP officer. Were the 13 agents, as we now know them, involved in other subversive activities in Canada?

subtopic: EXPULSION OF SOVIET UNION DIPLOMATS AND EMBASSY

Mr. Speaker, I am advised that all of the parties whose names I revealed today were associated exclusively with this one particular action whose sole objective was to penetrate the RCMP Security Services and establish within those services someone whom they regarded as being a reliable


source of information. My statement makes the point that it is an indication of the important the Soviets attached to this there were so many people involved. 1 have no doubt that the RCMP would be prepared to provide certain information as to the roles played by certain of these parties. I can, however, tell the hon. member in a general way that there was a central person involved who was the principal contact. Many of the others were involved in transportation, in the identification of signals, and in various other activities related to and part of the establishment of the two-way contact. I am perfectly satisfied that all were involved and that they were involved in this particular matter.

speechtext: In the year between February, 1976, and January, 1977, during which time, according to the minister's statement, the RCMP was aware of some of these happenings, the minister's own department granted 908 special travel permits to diplomats from the Soviet embassy to travel in parts of Canada other than the national capital region, including 41 special travel permits to the principal agent named today, Mr. Vartania. Eighty-eight were granted to Mr. Veber. The total number granted is 908. I wonder, if the RCMP was in the know with regard to these activities over the last year, why was the minister's department giving these individuals travel permits with such frequency and permitting them to travel outside the national capital area where surveillance obviously would be far more difficult?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yes, the hon. member has it exactly. The remainder were, what I might describe as, supporting players who unquestionably had breached their status as diplomatic persons within Canada but whose offence, if one wishes to use that word, was not of the same magnitude as that of the four principals involved.

Mr. Speaker, the number on strength at the Soviet embassy is 64, as approved by us under the international rules of procedure. maintopic: AMENDMENT TO CHANGE NAME OF RIDING OF HOCHELAGA-MAISONNEUVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of those two bills is to reestablish historical relevance in the designation of the new ridings of Hochelaga and Maisonneuve. The new riding named Hochelaga covers in fact the territory formerly known as the Sainte-Marie district. The history of the city of Montreal at the time of confederation shows us that that territory has always been designated under the name of Sainte-Marie from the very beginning. As for the village of Hochelaga, it was annexed to the city of Montreal in 1883, and its territorial limits are now included in the new riding of Maisonneuve. The purpose of those bills is therefore to respect historical relevance in the designation of those new ridings.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that the adoption of those bills will cause particular difficulties, even if the word "Hochelaga" means in the Huron language "place where one is caught in ambush".

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to say a few words respecting the amendment to Bill C-1001 which is before the House. Unfortunately it will be a few words because I have only 20 minutes. I would like to enlighten my more Conservative friends as to the merits of publicly owned telephones, but with only 20 minutes it is very difficult to list all of the attributes of public ownership when it comes to the telephone system.
1 am pleased that the first comment given was by a member from British Columbia. Before he disappears from the House I want to say to him that I have an article here from the Toronto Globe and Mail which says that the highest telephone rates in the country are those charged in British Columbia, in central Canada and in the maritimes. The lowest telephone rates in the country, as the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) knows, are the rates charged in the prairie prov-
Bell Canada
inces. You will note that all telephone systems operating in the prairie provinces are publicly owned. In instances where the telephone systems are privately owned, the rates are all very high indeed, and that speaks for itself. A publicly-owned telephone system is much more efficient, it provides a service at a much lower rate to the consumers, be they businessmen or private residential consumers.
I hope during this debate that Conservative members, particularly those from the prairies, the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski), the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar as well as others, will join in the debate and urge the federal government to place the Bell Telephone company under public ownership, as are the telephone systems operating in the prairies.
The bill that is before us today states that Bell Telephone want to expand their company, they want extra capitalization, and they want to make some changes in the legislation so that they would not have to come before parliament as often as they have done in the past. The amendment that is before us is to give that a six months' hoist.
I do not think that any of us should be rushing this bill through the House. First of all, Mr. Speaker, we notice in the press just a week or so ago that Bell Telephone are applying to the CRTC for a rate application increase of some $399 million. This is an application made by a company that has experienced large profits over the last many decades directly from the Canadian taxpayers. The rate increase will be 20 per cent for residences-and the Conservative party members laugh, they think it is great.

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext: It is the Liberals who are laughing.

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish that the electronic equipment in this House could record the laughs of the Conservative party as they laugh at the increase which is to be inflicted on consumers by Bell Telephone. Business rates are being increased by some 28 per cent commencing July 15, 1978. When we see rate increases like that, Mr. Speaker, I am in no hurry to allow Bell Canada to have their way and to see their bill go through this House in an expeditious manner.
1 wish the Conservatives who are now talking would get up from sitting on their brains and join this debate, it would be very interesting to hear their comments. People from Alberta, who have a socialized telephone system, should get up and tell us of the advantages of that socialized telephone system. There is another member who I would be very interested to hear speak, the progressive hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. He used to work for the Manitoba Telephone Company, which is publicly owned. That telephone company was established in Manitoba years ago by a great socialist, Premier Bracken. It is a telephone system which has worked very well. It will stay public even though the Conservatives are back in power in Manitoba. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) should be telling us how a socialized telephone system works and how the people of Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia should have a socialized system.


Bell Canada
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) will probably get up and tell us about the merits of public ownership of the telephone system in the province of Alberta. However, I am very concerned about the monopoly that Bell Canada has in this part of Canada. I am very concerned about the argument they are making to the CRTC for a rate increase.
In 1974, Bell Telephone made the argument that they needed to make between 11 per cent and 12 per cent profit in order to keep the company going. I gather they have been making that. Now they argue they need between W/2 per cent and 14i4 per cent profit to maintain and expand the system, attract new shareholder investment, modernize the company, modernize the equipment, and provide service to people living in outlying areas, northern areas and other parts of the country.
If we do not protest in this House, Bell Telephone will very easily get their way with the CRTC. Their batting average is very good. It is worth while to put on record the batting average of Bell Telephone since 1970, the last seven or so years they have gone before government regulatory agencies. I will go back over the last six.
In June, 1970, Bell requested some $30 million in terms of increases from the federal government. In January, 1971, they were granted $22.5 million, 75 per cent of what they were requesting. In November, 1971, Bell requested $78.1 million. In June, 1972, they were granted $47.2 million, 60 per cent of what they had requested. In November, 1972, they requested $36 million. In July, 1973, they were granted $22.5 million, 63 per cent of what they requested.
In August, 1973, Bell requested $51.8 million. Here I am talking of a company that charges its consumers the highest rates in the country for telephone service for residences and businesses. In September, 1974, they were granted $51.8 million, 100 per cent of their request.
In May, 1975, Bell requested $110 million. In August, 1975, they were granted $14 million, and in January, 1976, they were granted $96 million, again 100 per cent of what they had requested. In November, 1976, Bell again requested money, this time $171.4 million. In June, 1977, they were granted $162 million or 95 per cent of what they had requested of their clients in central Canada and the Atlantic provinces.
If you total that up, you find that since June, 1970, they have requested $477.3 million of which they have been granted $416 million, or 87 per cent of what they requested.
Bell Telephone wants to raise the rates for consumers in Ontario, Quebec and other places by 20 per cent in 1978. The chances of that increase going through are very high because over the past six or seven years they have received 87 per cent of what they requested. We have heard barely a whimper from the government members or members of the Conservative party about these excessive rate increases by Bell Telephone Company.

I can go over the financial reports of Bell Telephone in detail and look at their annual profits. Being a large monopoly corporation, it makes a lot of money. Despite the fact that they claim poverty and state that they need another rate increase, I have recently found that Bell Telephone will be investing a lot of money in Saudi Arabia. During the month of January, Bell Telephone won a billion dollar contract to upgrade the telephone system in Saudi Arabia. If they can expand their empire outside the country in places like Saudi Arabia where there is no shortage of money or technological skills, surely they can provide better telephone service in this country, primarily to those in our rural areas, northern areas where many people are on one line and repair service is very slow, and in residential areas.
When I moved into a new area, I had to wait literally weeks before my telephone was installed. For a while it was necessary to share a telephone line with someone else. Over the years I have not had any problems getting telephones installed in my residences in Saskatchewan. I have never had a constituent call me, write to me or stop me on the street to say that the Saskatchewan government telephone company is being lax or slow in a needless way with regard to installing telephones in either a residence or business.
I am sure all members from Saskatchewan, a province where the population has grown in the last seven years since the NDP government was elected, have not received complaints about the telephone system. The same is probably true in the province of Manitoba. However, here Bell Telephone has a monopoly. There is virtually little public control being exercised. They do what they want in terms of consumers, generally kicking them around. They are only interested in profit, not in providing a service to the people of this country.
When the rate increase application came up and the lawyers for Bell were preparing to argue their case before the CRTC, an article appeared in the February 3 issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail headlined "Metro Rate Would Be Twice Winnipeg's". The telephone rate in Toronto would be twice as high as in the city of Winnipeg. There are other rates that are three times as high as those in provinces where the telephone system is publicly owned.
I want to read some of the article so that hon. members will be aware of it and perhaps aid us in ensuring that we do not facilitate and expedite passage of the bill before us. I quote:
If Bell Canada has its way, a resident of some centres near metro Toronto soon will be paying three times as much lor basic telephone service as residents of Portage la Prairie, Manitoba, and Toronto residents will be paying double the rate in effect in Winnipeg.
A Globe and Mail survey of telephone rates in effect in seven metropolitan areas and seven small towns across Canada suggests that charges proposed in a Bell rate application now before the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission will be among the highest anywhere in Canada.
The survey showed that phone service for businesses and residences alike now is costliest in British Columbia and the maritimes and cheapest on the prairies.
Some of the differences are enormous. Among the cities, the charge for a private-line telephone service now ranges from a low of $4.00 in Winnipeg to a high of $9.95 in Halifax. Bell's charge in both Toronto and Montreal now is $8.15 but under the CRTC application would be $9.80.


Under the CRTC application the rate would go from $8.15 to $9.80. As I say, it is $4.90 in the city of Winnipeg-exactly half of what it is proposed Torontonians shall pay.
The articles goes on to say:
Residents of Portage la Prairie now pay $4 a month for basic phone service compared with a high of $10.25 a month in Bolton, Nobleton and parts of Pickering that can call free to Metro Toronto.
Of course, you could do the same thing from Portage la Prairie into Winnipeg as can be done between Pickering and Toronto.
The article goes on:
The same Metro-fringe Bell subscribers would pay $12.25 under the Bell proposal.
A barber in Portage la Prairie is billed only $8.75 a month for a business telephone. In Bolton the charge is now $31 and will jump to $39.70 if Bell's proposal is approved by the CRTC.
One could go on and quote at great length from the article in the Toronto Globe and Mail, because other examples are given about cities and rate comparisons across the country. Mention is made of Halifax and Regina, Portage la Prairie and Montreal. On previous occasions in debate I have given comparisons between cities like Moncton, Ottawa, etc. We find that in every case the rates charged by Bell Canada are substantially higher than the rates charged in my native province and its sister provinces of Alberta and Manitoba.
I have told the House that the rate in Winnipeg is $4.90. The comparable rate in my home province and capital of Regina is $5.45. I assume it is the same in the city of Saskatoon. 1 see no reason, therefore, why members of this House should give more power to Bell Canada. I see no reason why members of the House should give up what little scrutinizing ability we do have with respect to Bell. I do not see why Bell Canada should get our stamp of approval to secure a rate increase or expand the size of the corporation. The time has come to look realistically at ways of helping people and at the services we should offer.
Sometimes the best way of doing this is to establish publicly-owned companies. If a company is publicly-owned-and the communications field is a good example of where this should be done-then you can be sure that the sole motivation of such a company will be service to people. If a company is privately-owned, then normally its motivation will be to secure profits for its shareholders, not service to the people. For a privately-owned company there is no advantage at all in improving its facilities in outlying areas. In the hinterland areas, the rural communities far from villages and towns, there is no profit in improving the service.
Under the system which exists in Saskatchewan where an efficient, government-run telephone service is available, one which despite low rates has made a profit, you have a system of cross-subsidization. You can make a big profit in Regina or Saskatoon and use part of that profit to subsidize rates in the little towns and villages throughout the province. This is possible because the main motivating factor in the company is to serve people and to provide telephone service at the lowest
Bell Canada
possible cost. It will not be done by Bell Canada. It will not be done because Bell wants to make profits so it can invest money in Saudi Arabia or in other industries and make money for its shareholders.
Something else which I feel should be said at this time is that Bell Canada has made a great deal of money over the last number of years. It has done very well indeed. It has made a lot of money in this part of Canada and in the Atlantic provinces. We in our party, during the period in which this bill has been before the House, have drawn attention to some of the profits made by Bell. We have also outlined the manner in which the company treats some of its executives. Some of my colleagues have put on record details of the generous pension plans for some of the senior executives; they have put on record the amounts of some of the bonuses these senior people have received. Things like this just would not happen under a publicly-owned telephone system which was being run at the lowest possible cost for the best possible service to the greatest number of people.
These are just a few of the reasons why I call on all hon. members to oppose the bill before us as vigorously as possible.

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext: Bring it to a vote!

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext:
I see some Conservatives want us to bring the bill to a vote. I do not think we should bring it to a vote. The quicker we do that, the clearer the signal we give to the CRTC that we want a rate increase granted to Bell Canada. I know that members of the Conservative party from Saskatchewan probably do not want to do that. I also know that certain members from other parts of the country who do not know how a good telephone system should operate really believe Bell Canada needs the money the rate increases would provide. I am in no rush whatever to bring the bill to a vote, and I am sure other colleagues of mine who will be speaking later will take the same position as I.
I call upon the House to defeat the bill and to speak in the debate as long as they can in order to make sure that the people running Bell know we are concerned, that before they get any more handouts from us they will have to improve the services they provide to the people over whom they have a monopoly. Should this measure come to a vote before the next election, Mr. Speaker, the government-

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext: Order. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired. The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen).

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I just wish to remind the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) that in his opening remarks he said he had some things to say to me before I left the chamber. I want to say that even after listening to his jaded and jaundiced remarks for 20 minutes, I am still here-difficult as it was to listen to him-and 1 will still be here at six o'clock. He drew attention to how much money he is saving through the Saskatchewan Telephone Company. Obviously he took those savings and


Bell Canada
spent them on a vacation either in Florida or Cuba. Somehow or other he got that tan.

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters).

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members should not get up and apologize for it not being their day in the House; that happens to everybody at times but I do not think they have to apologize.
Bell Canada is a very important operation and one which deserves attention from the House. If members believe this, I hope they will be prepared to vote against the bill before us. This measure provides, among other things, for a change of great significance. Instead of parliament controlling Bell Canda, the cabinet is to do so by means of orders in council flowing from an application for changes in the organization of Bell by letters patent. These letters patent would be referred to the cabinet for decision. It is true there is a suggestion there might be an intervention on the part of members asking for a debate. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the result would be an overwhelming stamp of approval by Liberal members because the cabinet was involved.
We are going to try to hold this bill up until an election is called. After an election there will be no rubber stamping because there is obviously going to be a minority government. With a minority government all hon. members have to participate and justify their position.

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext: All six of you!

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext:
There may very well only be six and I hope I am one of them. I am not prepared to say whether it will be a Conservative government or a Liberal government. I am not too optimistic about it being an NDP government, but I am very optimistic that, no matter which party forms the government, the NDP is going to make the decisions. My assessment is that it will be a Conservative government and that we will make the decisions for them as we have sometimes for the Liberals.
Many hon. members believe we should pass this bill because Bell Canada can do nothing wrong. These members are mainly from western Canada where telephone service does not cost too much. In fact, in the three prairie provinces the telephone service is operated by the governments, through commissions. They assess public demand, calculate the costs and establish the rate to be charged. As my colleague pointed out, in some cases this amounts to less than half the charge in other areas.
Some hon. members will claim that free enterprise is a good system and that it pays. Many people in this country are opposed, however, to paying all the time and now want service at cost. They do not mind paying something for administration as long as it is not unreasonable. Where the telephone service is provided by commissions the costs are not exorbitant, as they are when Bell Canada provides it.

Bell Canada admits it is not really a telephone company. It owns some telephone companies-Northern Telephone in northern Ontario, Maritime Telephone and some others. I am sure they operate their subsidiaries pretty well as telephone companies, but the profits go back to Bell. They own Northern Telecom Limited, New Brunswick Telephone, Maritime Telephone, Newfoundland Telephone and Capital Telephone in the Ottawa area which, although it has less than 2,000 subscribers, owns Place Bell Canada, a fleet of ships and a jet air fleet. The subscribers have not had a rate increase for years and will probably never have one. If one were proposed, some subscriber would probably take it up with the CRTC. The company operates many things that have no relationship to a telephone service.
The Ottawa Citizen of March 9, 1977 quotes the president of Bell Canada as saying the company is a telecommunications operation and not just a phone company. Mr. Speaker, if 1 subscribe to Reader's Digest I expect to receive a magazine. I am not subscribing to those coupons that offer books or a lottery ticket for a million dollar prize. In my opinion you subscribe only to that in which you are interested. Many people subscribe to Bell Canada who only want a telephone, not a telecommunications network. They are not interested in buying other corporations that may be directly or indirectly connected with telephone communications. Why should a telephone company own boats, for instance? Some years ago when there was an international cable company and ships were required to service the cable this may have been necessary. Is it necessary today, however? The ownership of jet aircraft is not necessary in order to maintain a telephone service. Yet Capital Telephone owns some and rents them to other companies, including Bell Canada and its telecommunications services.
Bell Canada recently requested the CRTC to allow it to increase its rates, and not only to maintain the level of return it has been receiving. When the company went before the CRTC last year Andrew Roman, an intervener representing the National Anti-Poverty Organization, said he was concerned that the proposed increases would not be used to improve services to the ordinary telephone user but to facilitate company investment in non-voice data transmission for businesses. He said he had nothing against those services but that a rate increase should not be used to develop this nonvoice data transmission service at the expense of the ordinary telephone user.
At the hearing, questions were put by Mr. Dan Burtnick, a lawyer appearing for the government of Ontario, aimed at finding out from the president of Bell Canada whether his priorities lay with voice services or data services and where he would cut services if that were essential. In response, Mr. Thackray said that Bell Canada treated all its customers alike and did not give priority to the ordinary telephone user over data customers. He said that the Bell Canada act directed the company to provide telephones, but did not mention data services which did not exist when the act was passed. However, he insisted that the company was a telecommunications operation and not just a telephone company.


Also he said that the volume of data services offered by Bell Canada would likely increase relative to the volume of voice communication, and revenues from data might correspondingly increase in importance to the company. He continued by indicating that if Bell Canada did not get its rate increases, the company would cut back on services to private homes, because this was one of the quickest ways to stop spending money in the short term. He indicated that in doing this the company would be following the same course it had followed in 1975 when rate increases were held back.
Hon. members opposite must wear rose coloured glasses. They have indicated that Bell Canada should receive what it is requesting because it is necessary to maintain a good telephone communications system in Canada. Even the president of Bell Canada has indicated that the money will not be used to the benefit of ordinary telephone users. He has said that it will be used to make considerable money for Bell Canada.
It has been suggested that the New Democratic Party is interested in nationalizing Bell Canada. That is correct; we would like to do that because it is a public utility. These funds should be used to provide a service to the entire Canadian population, rather than the many ventures Bell Canada is now involved in.
There is a great similarity between the financial report of Bell Canada and that of the Canadian National Railways. The CNR is nationalized, but parliament has exercised very little control over it for many years. There has been control exercised by cabinet, and quite often the CNR was asked to do things it was not compensated for and did not wish to do. This was not the case with Bell Canada. That company has done things it wished rather than things which were requested by the cabinet or parliament. Bell Canada has had a greater interest in the role of the shareholder than that of the subscriber.
It has been recommended that the CNR should reduce its phony paper debt, a debt it was not capable of handling. That debt should have been written off a long time ago as any other such debt would have been. There have been very few years when the CNR has shown a profit. This year Canadian National is bragging about a $11 million profit. The last time the CNR debt was studied in committee, there was a deficit of $40 million and the interest on that debt was approximately $60 million. If the CNR had written off that debt, in that year the corporation would have earned $28 million in clear profit. Hon. members opposite have not paid much attention to the financial aspects of agencies under their control. This is also true of the agencies which have handled the rate structure of Bell Canada.
This year Bell Canada is requesting a 25 per cent increase. What is that company saying to the average person in Canada? Frankly, the public is not interested in giving Bell Canada that increase, but representatives of Bell Canada have said: "If you do not give it to us, none of the new suburbs will have telephones; we will not make any installations; and if you want to upgrade your telephone service, we will not do it".
Bell Canada
The subscribers in rural areas are the worst abused by Bell Canada, and they will suffer even further if Bell Canada does not receive its increase. It has been argued that it is costly to supply rural telephones, which is not true. For example, the majority of the expense involved in providing a telephone system to the rural areas of Saskatchewan took place a number of years ago, but that service was installed at a rate which was 100 per cent less than Bell Canada's rate for installing thousands of telephones back to back in an apartment building. In many instances Bell Canada is not required to use 20 feet of cable when installing telephones in apartment buildings.
In the city of Ottawa, where the lots are approximately 50 feet apart, Bell Canada requires approximately 30, 40 or 50 feet of coaxial cable per unit. That cable is buried in the ground and the contractor is required to do the installation during construction. All the telephone company has to do is to make the appropriate connections and instal the telephones. Yet some people in Ottawa have been waiting a long time for telephones. They are waiting for telephones because the company has indicated that it cannot make those connections until it is in receipt of the rate increase. The public is being blackmailed by this company.
What does Bell Canada tell the general public about its business? It tells them about the widows and orphans who own Bell Canada stock and, for that reason, the stock must be kept viable and the amount of dividends on those stocks must be in line with our national inflationary rate so that the poor widows and orphans will not starve to death. I should like to point out that I have a list of Bell Canada shareholders in my possession.

speechtext:
I am happy for that interjection. I invite the hon. member to interject more often because his interjections give me an opportunity to point out how badly the free enterprise system is working for his constituents. The hon. member does not want to listen. He is leaving the chamber.
Let us look at the record of the free enterprise system in which Bell Canada operates. I would like to quote some figures which were printed in the Globe and Mail. That newspaper is not a radical socialist journal. An article on February 3 of this year showed that the rate for an individual residential telephone in Winnipeg was $4.90 a month. In Regina it was $5.45, and in Calgary, $6.10. The present rate in Toronto for that same kind of line is $8.15 a month. If Bell gets the increase it is now asking for, the rate will be $9.80 a month. In Vancouver where there is also a privately-owned telephone company the rate at the present time is $9.75 a month, and in Halifax the rate is $9.95 a month.

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext: What are the labour rates in B.C. and in Manitoba?

subsubtopic: BELL CANADA
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) that the labour rate in Winnipeg is not one half the labour rate in Vancouver. That is not the reason for the sharp difference in price.
The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) referred to rates in small towns. In Portage la Prairie the rate for an individual residential line is $4 a month. In Bolton, Ontario, a town about the same size, the rate is $10.20. If Bell gets the increase it is asking for, the rate at Bolton will be $12.25. Those figures demonstrate very clearly why even free enterprise governments in the western provinces realize that, when it comes to services people require, it makes sense to have a publicly-owned system rather than a privately-owned monopoly system like that of Bell Canada.
Bell Canada is asking for an increase of between 20 per cent and 28 per cent. Bell is able to get approval 90 per cent of the time from regulatory agencies. The old one was the Canadian Transport Commission, and the present one is the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission.
We in the New Democratic Party have been blocking this bill, and we promise members of parliament and the executives of Bell Canada that we will continue to block it as long as the rules permit.
This bill would make the increases Bell has been able to get almost every year since I came to parliament in 1962 look like small fish in a big tank. Bell wants to remove the limited authority parliament has to keep an eye on what it proposes to do. It wants to remove most of the power of the CRTC. The bill would give Bell the authority to do everything which private companies operating in a competitive market are able to do. Bell wants to be able to sell shares, set the price of the

shares it sells, set up more subsidiaries, as it has already done, and operate with no government control at all. The company wants to increase its profit at a tremendous rate at the expense of the people of Canada. Bell Canada has a monopoly and is not in the same position as an ordinary private company which competes on the market with competitors here and abroad. An ordinary company risks losing money and going bankrupt but, being a monopoly, Bell does not.
This bill proposes a number of distinct amendments to Bell's act of incorporation. It would revise the act of incorporation relating to the company's ability and methodology of capitalization, including the removal of the scrutiny of the appropriate government regulatory body. That is something we will never agree to. If the bill is passed, it will give Bell the power to borrow and issue stocks, bonds, debentures or other securities that it deems necessary.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hate to quote a remark made either today or yesterday, but I find that in respect to this bill I will have to repeat a phrase which the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) used in this House. The more I read about this particular piece of legislation the more it becomes curiouser and curiouser. If one took a walk through the fairyland of economics, this would be the boulevard of all walking areas when looking at the history of the CNR.
It seems rather strange that people still ask for crown corporations in view of the history of this organization. How


many times it has been refinanced is a matter of some minor dispute. Some say four and some say five. I suppose it depends on whether you refer to the assumption of debt as the various lines were incorporated into the CNR and whether there was a little written off then. Anyway, I find it very startling to take a look at the record of write-offs which the CNR has experienced.
While it may be repetitive, it is significant to note that governments of Canada in their wisdom of four different occasions have chosen to relieve the CNR of debt to a degree that should make it competitive with other instruments of transportation. On each of the three times prior to this one it has failed utterly. For example, in 1933, under the guise of one excuse or other, we forgave the CNR a debt of $1,230 million. At that time the CNR was supposed to be competitive.
In 1937 we eliminated a debt to the tune of $1,000,825. That is quite a hunk of change. It was particularly large coming just four years after the forgiveness of $1,230 million. In 1937 we therefore had nearly S3 billion of indebtedness that had been forgiven for a Crown corporation. To those who plead for Crown entities operated and financed by the taxpayer, that ought to be an initial lesson of its total lack of vision and capability.
In 1952 there was a further forgiveness of debt and interest which amounted to $2,845 million. In 1978 we are forgiving an additional $808 million, which will bring us to the point of having forgiven $6,708 million.
There is another Crown corporation owned and operated by the government of Canada which is building up a comparable structure of debt which was also forgiven by this government. I refer to the Seaway, which is another example of where the
taxpayers have had to fork over in order to keep a Crown corporation in operation. I am just sick of Crown corporations.
I submit there is a better way.
Thirty years ago rail rates were giving the Atlantic area problems in two ways. They were going up so fast that it made it difficult for producers to ship westward to Canadian markets. The Atlantic area was not developing at that time. We have had a meteor-like rise in rates in the past 30 years to the point where the income of producers in the Atlantic area has been further diminished. Our competitive position, particularly as it relates to agriculture, has been virtually wiped out. The advantages of expertise, soil in agriculture, yield and climate, have been literally totally wiped out. We now find ourselves in a position of disadvantage. Producers of those commodities which at one time were profitable are now at a disadvantage by virtue of the fact that this Crown corporation has led the way in the increment of freight rates from the Atlantic area to western markets.
We are now forgiving another $800 million indebtedness which brings the total relief given by the taxpayers to the CNR to $6.7 billion. Yet we still do not have a competitive position for our products in the Atlantic area.
There is a further problem. Not only has our income been reduced by virtue of railway tariff increments, but our cost of
Railway Act
living has increased as charges levied by one Crown corporation after another in the movement of goods from west to east have increased. Therefore, we are getting it both ways; there is a reduction in income on that which we ship, and there is an increasing demand on our income and cost of living to pay for goods which cost us more because of freight charges which are increased on about a six monthly basis. As a maritimer being taken both coming and going, I am not really very happy about forgiving a further $800 million to the CNR.
I am particularly unhappy when I look at the CNR financial statement. It shows a long-term debt of $2,238 million. We are going to forgive $808 million of that. CN will still be $1.4 billion in debt.
I am even more unhappy when I look at remarks made at an earlier date when one of these forgiveness festivities took place. A gentleman known to many people in this House by the name of Mr. Donald Gordon said in a message to CN employees after the forgiveness of 1952 that we are now in a position where we have nothing to hide behind, nothing to block the road to success. He stated that we have a fighting chance of paying our way in the world and that, counting the bad years with the good, we ought to be able on the average to pay all our operating expenses, our fixed interest charges and income taxes and still have something left to return to the owners as a dividend on preferred stock.
In the 25 years since that assessment of its prospects, the CN system incurred net debts totalling $670 million, paid by the government, despite an infusion of $768 million of capital through government purchase of preferred stock which added more than $1 billion to its long-term debt, separate and apart from the financing of Air Canada. CN's fixed charges grew from $25 million to $132 million in the period 1952 to 1957.
I remember a very heated debate on a bill surrounding the establishment of the CN Tower in Toronto. At the time that tower was being proposed and while it was being constructed, it was criticized for taking money away that was badly needed for rolling stock and other items in the business of CN. It may or may not have been a profitable structure. I am not able to determine whether it is, except for a few government words and a few railroad official words which indicate something about it. In any event, whether it is profitable is not yet clear.
What is clear is that CN has been interested in a great many things other than transportation. When it was incapable of managing its principal business, it was permitted to go afield into real estate, towers, airplanes, hotels and a multitude of different services. It does this despite the fact it was not even capable of running the railroad first. The government has encouraged and allowed this structure to become diversified although this Crown corporation could not manage what it already had. This Crown corporation had proved itself incompetent ever since it was incorporated as such. I predict this will probably not be the last time members of the House will be asked to discuss refinancing the CNR and making further sums available to the company.


Railway Act
I would point out that the indebtedness remains at $1.4 billion. In earlier times when forgiveness was sought from parliament, it was said that the company had inherited massive debts, that it had been asked by government to do things which a private corporation would not be asked to do and it was therefore necessary to ask parliament for a little more money to put the railway back into competitive shape. But the historic debt has more than been forgiven, Mr. Speaker. The existing debt of the CNR is probably comparable to that of other corporations operating in Canada. It is said the company has no equity capital. But why should it need equity capital when the government will pour into its coffers every nickel the company loses in a year's operation? Why should it need equity capital when the government is always ready to buy preferred shares upon which no interest is ever paid? It might be accrued but it is never paid. I contend it has befuddled the minds of Canadians by failure to adopt proper accounting procedures over the years. Why did the government not insist on knowing on an annual basis just how badly this corporation was operating as compared with private companies of a similar nature?
The country has been hoodwinked by the government and by the executive structure of the CNR into believing the company was nearly making a profit as taxpayers poured their millions into the sustenance of this corporation. Now we are being asked to forgive another $808 million, making $6.7 billion in total.
Reading various commentaries on the CNR one finds that people are making statements with respect to the extravagance of the capital expenditure. I have no instance of this extravagance. Every shipper of farm goods, whether he lives on the east or the west coast, knows that the car situation has been critical for years. The Government of Canada, in addition to the $6.7 billion, has had to buy cars to move grain though it has refused to buy cars to move perishable goods. It is a sorry record.
I am of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that during the consideration of this bill no one to your right should urge us to hurry this legislation through so as to get the CN on its feet. Do not hurry this time. We want an accurate accounting study to show us what is the true position of the CN in comparison with that of its principal competitor, CP. What is the competitive position of the CNR in the area of road transportation? What is its competitive position in the area of water transportation? Until such time as the minister is prepared to give us authentic figures of this kind I do not think it would be fair to the taxpayers that any member on Your Honour's right should say at any point in time that a member of the opposition is holding up this bill. It is time the government and its child, the CNR, levelled with the people of Canada. We need to know these facts from experts who might have some idea what they are- and I mean from sources outside of government.
Another piece of legislation we are considering, the Aeronautics Act, shows that the Department of Transport has no idea what is going on. Take a look at the report. You will
find out we collected certain funds from aircraft operations and then reimbursed them again. We are trying again to collect them now and we probably cannot win, because according to the advice the Department of Justice received, a regulation may not have been correctly worded or the act was improperly framed. Sure as anything it was improperly administered; the story is that for ten years the department wanted to get an amendment through, but the government has not given time or space in its schedule for a new aeronautics bill to be brought in. So the position with regard to that is one of total confusion. If the administration of the CNR and the Department of Transport is as dismal as it has been in the case of Air Canada, then Canada needs to know. We need to know what is the competitive position.
We do know that there will be demands on the CNR for cars for the shipment of perishable goods. There will be demands for cars for the prompt shipment of frozen foods, demands for cars for the prompt shipment of all kinds of goods and commodities. What is the total of these anticipated demands likely to be? What are likely to be the capital requirements of the CNR? Will the company be able to buy these cars and haul goods from one part of Canada to another at a price we can afford? What impact will this have on rates? As a maritimer I am concerned about this aspect.
In our last discussion of the cost of transportation in the Atlantic area my remarks involved a comparison of rates for the movement of wood products in the maritimes, particularly in New Brunswick, as compared with the cost of moving comparable products in British Columbia. I showed that in New Brunswick the CN was charging us anything from 25 per cent to 100 per cent more than the British Columbia railroad was charging to move such products in B.C.
At that time the B.C. railroad was making a profit. I admit there was a so-called government out there leaning a little to the left; it almost caused that enterprise to flounder, too. The only two governments which could be compared in business management would be that government and the one on your right, Mr. Speaker. We are now in a position where producers of wood, wood products and paper in New Brunswick are taking a look at competitive rates in the state of Maine. We find that in Maine there is an even wider differential when it comes to the movement of wood products than there was between rates in New Brunswick and British Columbia. It is even more unfavourable.
The CNR does not look very good, Mr. Speaker, and I can see no point in giving the company $808 million if this House is not assured by the minister and the department that there is likely to be in the foreseeable future sufficient management capability to ensure that we shall not be asked again to forgive a large portion of the railway's obligations. The Bible tells us we should turn the other cheek. Mr. Speaker, we have turned it, turned it and turned it-and we got slapped every time we turned. The minister from Restigouche can grin but he has potato producers in his constituency who are just not competitive with producers in central Canada today because of unfair freight rates charged by the only railway running through his



constituency, the CNR. So the minister had better be prepared to tell us some facts and give us some prospects for the future which would justify the taxpayers forgiving $808 million.
What a dismal history for a Crown corporation. Why do members opposite not stand up and cheer? I remember going to the railway station in my community thirty years ago. It had a roadbed with no grass then but there were some good ties and a crew of men went along its length repairing it. Today the grass in that road bed is so high that you could not tell whether there were any ties unless you took the trouble to dig. The speed limit on the line is 15 miles an hour. It is ten miles an hour in Prince Edward Island. There are not many rail points in Prince Edward Island where heavy produce can be loaded, and even at those you cannot be sure what kind of car will be used and whether the load will be safe. Yet this government takes no action and the CNR takes no action.
Just recently the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) received a telegram from the New Brunswick Potato Shippers Association about the situation in that industry. When the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) was in Grand Falls he received a deputation which stated that the industry could not be competitive if the CNR and the CPR did not take a realistic look at the value of transportation to industry, supply it with equipment and give it a rate that would enable it to survive.
Let us assume, Mr. Speaker, that you want to export potatoes from the constituency of Madawaska-Victoria. You might have the choice of loading them in Maine and shipping them through a port there or loading them in New Brunswick and shipping them through either Saint John or Halifax. The charges for going through the state of Maine would be somewhere between one-third and one half of the charges imposed by the CN or the CP. Now we are asked to forgive this debt and to smile while doing it. Mr. Speaker, it makes you cry crocodile tears.
It used to be the case that when you loaded a perishable commodity on the railway they had the responsibility to see to it-whether the weather be too hot or too cold-that the produce arrived at its destination in good condition. Now the government in its ignorance-and please note that I said ignorance, Mr. Speaker-has allowed the railroads to remove the priority for the movement of perishable products. Cars of potatoes, fruit and vegetables have been left sitting along the sidings in Canada until they rotted or froze, depending upon the weather. The CNR takes no responsibility for this. To the best of my knowledge and belief it is the only service in Canada for which the people have been asked to pay more and from which, on an annual basis, they have received less in the form of quality of equipment and service.
More and more producers in Atlantic Canada, agricultural or otherwise, are buying their own trucking outfits to move their goods to the markets of central Canada. This is not necessarily because it is cheaper or because they are making money on transportation-although they claim they are not
Railway Act
losing-but rather because the railway system cannot deliver to the satisfaction of the customer. When you cannot satisfy your customer, Mr. Speaker, you do not have any business. Small businesses are going into trucking because the railroads, particularly the CNR, cannot deliver to their satisfaction.
I am looking forward to the day when CNR officials will appear before this committee, and I hope the minister will insist that we be given an opportunity to get an in depth accounting of present conditions. I should like the company to explain why wood products can be moved more cheaply in Maine than in New Brunswick, for instance.
I want also to know what is the cost structure. A blind man could tell that the Problem is not only the difference in equipment, though ours could not deteriorate any further. Does the problem lie with despatching? History shows that we have forgiven all debts, so they do not have to worry about money.
On many occasions I have inquired if the Department of Transport has ever made a study of other railroads in the world that managed to make a profit and compared them with the CNR, but I have not been able to get answers. Just this morning I put a question to an official of the department and he began his reply "I would conjecture-". Mr. Speaker, we have had a lot of conjectures and they have been costly. I think it is time we had some definitive and accurate answers.
We believe we have placed great men in executive positions in the CNR. Is the present situation their fault, or the fault of the government which has imposed constrictions upon the CNR? Is it because of bad management? Where is the weakness, Mr. Speaker, that causes producers to turn to trucks?
I hope the minister will also explain the competitive position between rail and water transportation. Other carriers are being put at a disadvantage. We know that the Post Office has discriminated against part of the trucking industry through adopting a plan to carry small packages. I do not think it has done very much for the Post Office but it has taken business away from private enterprise.
Mr. Speaker, this type of transportation is important to Canada. There is not much use, however, in the government investing in DREE and other aid projects if there is no transportation system to take goods to market at a competitive price. It does not make any difference whether the money is invested in Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, New Brunswick or Nova Scotia, the product must go to market. If the goods cannot go through our ports at a price competitive with Maine, then they are not going to be competitive on the international market. If they cannot be moved to central Canada at a price competitive with other jurisdictions, then they are not going to be competitive with goods produced in the state of New York or the state of Washington.
I should like now to turn to CN Marine. As far as I know it is the only water transport structure that does not offer reasonable insurance protection for the vehicles it carries. The automatic coverage for a tractor-trailer carried on the CN


Railway Act
marine ferry on the east coast is $500. To recover more than that one must sue the Crown. No matter how you try you cannot get marine insurance for travel on that ferry because all too often the tractor-trailers are not secured well enough. Not long ago when the ferry hit a big wave, a tractor-trailer tipped over and crushed three cars. Then when they got it off those three cars it went the other way and crushed two more. This is not hearsay, this is fact. There were five automobile owners who were in a jam when they tried to collect insurance, and there is no truck owner who can get insurance which will come anywhere near covering the loss of upsetting his load first left and then right. They did a good job on that one! This is what makes one wonder about Crown corporations.
CN Marine has insurance, but the only way you can collect from that insurance is to sue the Crown of Canada. It is not good to operate a ferry in such a fashion. Companies cannot afford to pay marine insurance for the loads they put on that ferry and have to take the liability into their own hands and sue the Crown, or buy insurance at such a rate that a maximum value load might cost you $15,000 in freight to move it from Cape Breton to Newfoundland. It could actually cost as much as $15,000 to move one load. Therefore, the people who use that ferry service are paying their own bills or, if they are big enough, bold enough, patient enough, and have money enough, they sue the Crown.
Why do we as taxpayers have to forgive for a fourth and maybe a fifth time? Why do we not have a Department of Transport with the capability of extending businesslike management to a Crown corporation? That is what it needs. I am not accusing this government as a government, I am accusing all governments of Canada historically for contributing to this situation. I am pleading with this government-and I hope the people of Canada will insist on this-to put this corporation on a paying basis. We in Canada cannot afford to allow the CNR or any other railway to neglect its road bed because it cannot find the ties. Canadian producers do not have the money to produce products when they cannot find cars to ship them. Canadian taxpayers are being abused by the Department of Transport and its minister in a very great way. A boulevard of fantasy to a fairyland of economics is what this tragedy of economic history would seem to be.

I am not a Manitoban, I am a Saskatchewanian, and I point this out in reply to that interjection from across the floor.
In any event, the bill before us today gives us a very good opportunity to talk about transportation and the way the economy and the industries of our country should be organized, and it gives us a chance to talk about some of the inequities that exist in Canada. The transportation system is really a vital key to how one organizes the country.
The bill before us is to recapitalize the CNR by writing off $808 million of a debt of around $2 billion that the CNR had accumulated at the time it was formed. There are three different things I want to refer to tonight in the remarks I intend to make. The first is that our party supports the move. We believe that writing off the debt of the CNR is a good thing. We believe the CNR should be on an equal footing with the CPR so it can give that company some real competition.
The second thing I want to concern myself with is the real fear I have that this move, even though it is a good move, is the first step toward privatization of the CNR, turning it into a private company by selling it off piece by piece, particularly the profitable areas, to private concerns and companies. I think that would be very wrong, Mr. Speaker.
My third concern when talking about a bill of this sort, to which I have already referred, is that we also talk a little about the transportation system of our country, how we plan it; we should talk about industrial strategy and how we want our country to be organized.
Let me have a look at the history of railways in our country. As I have said already, the move in itself is a good one. The CNR has been criticized very unfairly for a number of years as being a very inefficient corporation. The CNR has really been very efficient. If you go back to the time of World War II, Mr. Speaker, you find that the CNR really made a profit in almost all of those years; that is, if you take away some of the horrendous debt it has and the interest it had to pay on that debt which it inherited.


The CPR has always been in a different situation. It was subsidized very heavily by Canadian governments over the years, and as a result of that it is basically debt free compared to the CN.
