Let me look at some of the facts. When the CPR was formed it was given $25 million in cash on an outright gift basis; it was given some 25 million acres of land; it was given other private railways that became part of the CPR in our country, and it was given all kinds of various rights and gifts by the federal government of this country. It is now worth about $5 billion, which is a lot of money.
The CPR has also been able to expand into several other businesses in our country. It is involved in land development through Marathon Realty; it is involved in the airline business through CP Air; it is involved in the resource industry through Cominco; it is involved in oil through CP Oil; and it is involved in the financial world through CP Investments.
When we consider the CN we see the reverse situation. Instead of being given all kinds of gifts and subsidies, as was the CPR, we find that the CNR was really formed when five railways in this country went bankrupt-the Intercolonial Railway, the National Transcontinental Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway. In 1919 these five railway companies as well as a few tiny branch railways or companies were formed into the CNR. So that when the CNR was formed it was loaded down right away with all kinds of debts. As a result it has always been in a very disadvantageous position in terms of competition with the CPR.
I want to say at the outset that I am in favour of this bill, which will take away much of that debt from the CNR and put it on an equal footing with the CPR, giving it an equal chance to compete right across this country.
Let me now say a few words about my fear regarding the privatization of the CNR. From the statements I have heard from the president of the CNR, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and other officials of the railway and the government, one of the objectives is to gradually sell off the CN. They will start doing that by selling off the more profitable aspects of the railway; that is, by taking away some of its profitable branches. They have already set up VIA Rail and are now talking about reorganizing other branches of the CN, such as the hotel end, for example. They are talking about prying this aspect away from the company. I maintain this should not be done.
One amendment I should like to see would result in the shares of the CNR not being traded publicly but remaining 100 per cent owned by a Crown corporation. This would result in its being operated as a Crown corporation in a similar fashion to the Saskatchewan Power Corporation, the Sas-
Railway Act
katchewan government telephone company, the Saskatchewan insurance corporation and all kinds of other companies. This is the manner in which I would like to see the CNR operated, but it will not be done in that way.
There are many reasons why the CNR should remain a publicly-owned corporation. In fact, the CPR should be nationalized as well in order to have one national railway system in Canada. A transportation system should provide a basic service to people. It should not be in existence simply to provide a profit to its shareholders. If the railway system is publicly owned, then decent transportation will be provided to the various regions of our country. If that system is privately owned, its main concern will be the making of a profit. I do not believe in that, but it is the motivation of the free enterprise system.
Transportation should not be organized in that way. If it is, there will be greater concentrations of people in the huge urban centres such as southern Ontario, metropolitan Montreal and the lower mainland of British Columbia. At the same time there will be fewer people living in the farm regions, the small towns, the Atlantic provinces, the north and the other areas which are distant from the urban centres. People will gravitate toward the large centres if there is a privately owned transportation system, because transportation and freight rates will be lower.
If the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) and myself wanted to set up a shoe factory, we would do so in Toronto because it has the market and the freight rates are lower. Transportation should be organized in the opposite sense. It should be operated under a philosophy similar to that which governs the postage stamp. The postage stamp philosophy does not discriminate against people because of where they live. If a person lives in Inuvik and wants to send a letter to Ottawa, the cost will be the same as that for the person who wants to send one from Montreal to Ottawa: Some of that philosophy should be ingrained in the Canadian transportation and freight rate system.
If there was an equalization of freight rates in this country, a lot more would be done for the Atlantic provinces and the outlying areas than the DREE program is doing, for example. The DREE program is only good as long as the carrots or the gifts are there. When Santa Claus runs out of gifts, then there is no reason for DREE to stay in the place where it was established. Often it will fold up, or certainly it will not expand. If the freight rates were equalized from coast to coast, then there would be a reason for industry to stay and to expand.
I, as well as many other hon. members from the prairies, can give various examples of discriminatory freight rates and their effect upon the prairies provinces. Some commodities can be shipped more cheaply from Toronto and Hamilton to Vancouver than they can be shipped from Toronto to the prairies provinces. It is cheaper to ship certain goods overseas than it is to ship certain goods to the prairies because the transportation


Railway Act
system is in the hands of large companies which are interested in making profits. There is no competition for those companies in the prairies. Thus, they have a monopoly and can charge what the market will bear. That is another reason why 1 believe the Canadian transportation system should be publicly owned and operated on behalf of all people.
I hope parts of the CNR are not sold off. If they are, the ones sold will be the profitable ones and the ones retained will be those which are losing money. The Liberal government has viewed Crown corporations over the years as follows: if it is profitable, sell it because it can be looked after by private companies; but if it is not profitable, then it should be subsidized by the treasury.
The transportation system should be an integrated system. It should be involved in the hotel business and be integrated with trucking companies, but companies and airlines. That would result in a national plan, and within the national transportation system, cross-subsidization could take place.
When the CCF took power in the province of Saskatchewan in 1944, one of its priorities was to ensure that small communities received bus service. Many villages, communities and hamlets received bus service because of that. They do not receive that service from Greyhound or some other private bus company because it does not pay to go into these small communities. They receive their bus service from the Saskatchewan Transportation Company, STC, which has been set up as a Crown corporation and is owned by the people of Saskatchewan.
The STC makes money on some of its lines, such as the run from Yorkton to Regina, which are large population centres. They are 115 to 120 miles apart. The STC is losing money on runs from Regina through little villages and hamlets, stopping every eight or ten miles. Sometimes the bus stops to pick up an old age pensioner who is going into the city; sometimes the bus stops to drop off a passenger who is going to visit someone in the next village or town. The Saskatchewan Transportation Company loses money on rural runs, but it uses the profits made on the busier runs to subsidize them. Without STC, rural communities would not have a bus service and they probably would be smaller today because there would be one less service for the people. But as a result of the publicly-owned bus system, these people have service. The only way that service could be profitable would be to charge excessively high rates, and then no one would use the service because of the cost. The example of the Saskatchewan Transportation Company could be expanded right across Canada.
In Yorkton and from time to time in Brandon, as is the case in Dauphin, Manitoba, there is a problem with inadequate air service because of the lack of population. Private companies do not want to provide air service to Yorkton and Dauphin because it does not pay. Thus, they cannot make a profit, nor can a dividend be paid to shareholders. The only way these communities will receive good air service is for a private company to be heavily subsidized, or for Air Canada to provide it. If a private company is going to be heavily subsidized, it might as well be publicly owned.
[Mr. Nystrom.)
If the CNR and the CPR were amalgamated and operated as a Crown corporation, then it could be used as a major planning device for our economy and would assist in diversif-ing our population. Most Canadians live in three or four of the larger population centres. This creates all kinds of problems in terms of crime rates, the noise of the big city, transportation problems, and hustle and bustle. Most of our big cities are built on the best farmland. Only one half of one per cent of Canada is class one farmland. If the urban centres are expanded, then more farmland is paved over. By taking away the grain and oilseeds industries, Canada will not be self-sufficient in the production of food.
For many reasons it makes sense to have a publicly owned transportation system which has as its motivation service to people and service to outlying areas instead of making a profit. Those are some of the matters which concern me about this bill.
Another conern is that if we do not have a publicly-owned transportation system, we will have to adopt the philosophy of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) of user-pay. If that philosophy is adopted, outlying areas will have to pay the bill. Farmers on the prairies will have to pay the bill for transporting their grain. The Crowsnest rate will probably disappear, and farmers will then have to pay the full cost of transporting their grain.

speechtext:
Many of us on the prairies say "never" and "over our dead bodies." I am sure it would be over the dead body of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) as well as mine, but the Minister of Transport does not say "never". Sometimes he says "maybe," particularly right after an election. Perhaps as we go into a campaign he says "never", but reading through his speeches I have found that he is seriously considering getting rid of the Crow rate. He says that perhaps farmers will be given the benefit of that rate in some other way, but the user pay philosophy means that farmers themselves will pay the full cost of shipping their grain.
One of the benefits the country was supposed to have reaped from the CPR when that company got concessions from the public years ago was that the company was going to ship farmers' grain at a reduced rate forever. 1 am afraid that if we adopt the user-pay concept, that will not happen.
I want to discuss the issue of rail line abandonment. If we want railways to make money, we are obviously talking about abandoning unprofitable rail lines, rail lines which service small communities and which might not haul as much grain as rail lines which service communities in the big grain growing areas of the prairies. This issue affects many people in my area, and I want to spend a few minutes giving some specific examples.
The minister has talked for a long time about abandoning some rail lines. A commission chaired by Mr. Hall produced a



report on grain handling and transportation in western Canada. The Hall commission report was tabled a few months ago. It recommended a number of things with regard to railways and the prairies.
There are three lines in my riding which can perhaps illustrate the point I want to make. Mr. Hall divided railways into three categories. He said that about one-third of the rail lines should stay as part of the basic network. About another one-third are rail lines which it is suggested should go between now and the year 1981. The third group of lines is a group upon which the commission could not make a decision. They might be commercially viable but they might not. The commission feels that they should be the subject of further study. The commission recommended that those rail lines be put under the proposed prairie rail authority. The prairie rail authority is to make up its mind about the future of those lines. However, the minister has not yet established a prairie rail authority. He set up a committee, which is really an extension of his office, chaired by an individual in Saskatchewan, which is going to make recommendations on the future of rail lines in the country.
One of the prime factors in determining whether a rail line will go or stay is whether it is profitable. Because the Minister of Transport believes in the user pay concept. If the user is not paying enough, then the rail line will go. I would like to give three specific examples of what I mean.
There is a rail line in the northern part of my constituency which runs through the towns of Preeceville, Lintlaw, Nut Mountain and Kelvington and which hauls a lot of grain. That rail line should stay. The ten-year average on that line is about 73,000 bushels per mile. That is a lot of grain, and yet the minister is considering abandoning that line. A local committee from those communities was established a few months ago to save the line. They received a letter from the minister. If I remember correctly, that was on December 28. It was certainly toward the end of last year. That letter stated that in the following year a recommendation would be received from the prairie rail action committee about the future of that line. Unless the members of those communities fight really hard, my guess is that that line will go since the minister believes in the philosophy of user pay.
That philosophy discriminates against small towns and small communities. As Saskatchewan members know, places like Preeceville and Kelvington are not small towns, and when you haul 73,000 bushels of grain per mile on a railway track, that is not a small haul. It is a significant amount of grain. That line should stay, and it would stay if we had a rational transportation system, a system concerned about service to people rather than profit.
What is happening now-and I suspect that the minister is an accomplice to this-is that that line is being allowed to deteriorate. Snow is not being cleared off the line. It is getting run down. It is more and more difficult to argue that the line is viable, but that is part of the plan. The plan is to eliminate many rail lines in this country.
Railway Act
There is another line in my constituency which runs from the town of Canora through to the little town of MacNutt, which is near the Manitoba boarder, close to the riding of the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie). That is another line which might be going between now and 1990. There are about ten elevators on that line. In the years in between 1967 and 1975, 1975 being the year the Hall commission was appointed, about 1.6 million bushels of grain moved along that line. That is about 42,000 bushels of grain per mile of track. The line is some 37.8 miles long, and it services a number of small communities. They are very fragile communities because they are located quite close to larger centres like Dauphin, Yorkton, Kamsack and Canora. In the small centres, if the railway goes, their elevators go. If the elevators go, so go the agents and their families. Where there are schools, they might be the next to go. If the elevators go, the reason for farmers to come to these communities also goes. Farmers will shop elsewhere and those communities will die. I do not want to see that happen. It is already happening too much on the prairies and in rural Canada; it does not have to happen.
A third line in my riding to which I want to refer is not as fortunate as the previous two. According to the Hall Commission report and all the indications I have received from the minister, it will probably be abandoned some time between now and the end of 1981. This line services two small communities, Jedburgh and Willowbrook, and hauls about 34,000 bushels of grain per mile. Both these communities are small, but they are communities. They have community halls, stores and post offices. They have grain elevators, and if the elevators go-and according to the minister they will-it is only a matter of time before the communities die. It is only a matter of time before some of the small farmers go, because if they have to haul their grain further to get to an elevator, they will not survive in business. Larger operations will, but the small ones will be squeezed out. Large operations can afford to haul grain longer distances.
In many of these places the taxpayer will have to foot the bill. These communities are on roads which are not built to carry large amounts of grain in large trucks. If large trucks are used on these roads, the roads will be damaged and municipalities will have to spend much more money upgrading them and keeping them in shape. Once again, the ordinary people of those communities will be hit the hardest.
That is an example of the tragedy which will be caused by the user pay concept. It is an example of what I mean by the tragedy of always trying to make a profit, instead of having a transportation system which will serve the people of this country. If we had a transportation system that had as its priority service to the people, we would not have wholesale rail line abandonment across the prairies, and there would be some hope for the small prairie communities which are gradually going to dwindle away and disappear.
We now come to the question whether we can believe the government. Transportation has been an issue in our part of


Railway Act
the country for years. Before the debate this evening I searched for some statements made by the Minister of Transport and the Prime Minister in the last election campaign. This was in an effort to find any statement of hope for the people who live in those small communities I referred to in my riding and, also those who live in the ridings of almost any rural member from the prairies sitting in this House. I found that in the election campaign of 1974 the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport certainly fiddled and sang to a different tune than the tune they are singing now.
I will quote some statements that will prove that without any shadow of a doubt. First of all, I quote from the issue of the Winnipeg Free Press of June 8, 1974. 1 am sure this will be of interest to all Conservative candidates, and it is of interest to our candidates. It reads as follows:
Justice Minister Otto Lang told a public meeting Friday night that if the Liberal government is re-elected not one railway branch line on the prairies will be abandoned as long as producers deliver to elevators on the line and the elevators continue to operate.
In the same meeting he said, and I quote again:
Countering opposition that he is out to close the many small grain elevators situated close to farmers... he declared that the smaller elevators will, in effect, remain as long as farmers want them.
I serve notice on the Minister of Transport that in my riding there are three "save our rail" committees. In each of these three communities where these rural lines travel the people want those elevators, they want those branch lines, and the farmers will continue delivering to those elevators as long as the elevators are there. The elevator companies in some of these places have assured me that they have no intention at all, Mr. Speaker, of closing down the elevators. They will be there as long as the Minister of Transport makes sure the rail lines are there. I say to him: "Let us make sure that you live up to your promises". With another election coming the Minister of Transport will probably make those same promises again, so I remind him of the promises which he has made to the country.
Again, another statement from the Winnipeg Free Press of June 11, 1974:
Otto Lang said, "as long as the Liberal party forms the government and as long as producers wish to continue to deliver to the elevator of their choice, not one rail line will be abandoned."
Now I wish to quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of June 15, 1974, under the headline "Prime Minister Outlines Farm Policy". I did not know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) knew one cow from the other, but he was in Winnipeg and on June 15 he outlined the government's farm policy, according to this newspaper. The Prime Minister said:
He also reiterated his party's pledge to end any freight discrimination on the movement of meat, livestock and feed grains across Canada. This would not affect the Crowsnest special rates to aid the movement of grains for export to the west coast.
In that particular instance the Prime Minister is talking about saving the Crowsnest rate. I now quote from the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 15, 1974:
Justice Minister Otto Lang promised to pay farmers premium rates if they volunteer to take longer hauls, and to allow smaller grain elevators to stay in use as long as farmers want them.
As long as farmers want to use the grain elevators, they will stay in use, according to the Minister of Transport. I have a further quote from the Prime Minister saying approximately the same thing. This statement is also taken from the Toronto Globe and Mail of June 15, 1974:
He also added another plank to a transportation policy... He promised yesterday (June 14, 1974) not to abandon rail service on branch lines as long as elevator companies considered that continued rail service was warranted.
These are examples of campaign promises that were made in June, 1974, all of them to the effect that if farmers wanted to continue delivering grain to the elevators on the branch lines as I am sure they will in all of our ridings, not one elevator would be closed by the government of this country.
Let us make sure that the people who live in those areas know what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport have said. When the election campaign gets under way these promises will be heard again. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) will be adding his promises as well. We must be certain that the people do not make the same mistake again and re-elect those members to the House of Commons. If they do, abandonment of the rail lines on the prairies will come to pass.
All of us can pick up a copy of the Hall report, and we can see the maps of the railways, we can see the different colours of the lines and we can see quite visually which rail lines will be abandoned. When Mr. Justice Hall tabled his report, so clearly and well presented, it seemed to me that he did not want all of those rail lines abandoned; he wanted a prairie rail authority set up to study them further.
The indication I am getting is that most of those rail lines will be abandoned. I say to the people of Canada: "Let's put pressure on the minister for the few short months that he is going to be on his job". We must try to have him make a commitment to the effect that those rail lines will stay.
I see the hon. member for Crowfoot and the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) sitting across the way.

The minister is saying that he is not ashamed of the statements his colleagues in the cabinet have made. He must be embarrassed by what has been said by the Minister of Transport. I think it was the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who said at one time that the Minister of Transport should be tarred and feathered. I am sure he still believes that, and that he is a little embarrassed.
I return to this quote from the Winnipeg Free Press of June 8, 1974 which states:
Justice Minister Otto Lang told a public meeting Friday night that if the Liberal government is re-elected not one railway branch line on the prairies will be abandoned as long as producers deliver to elevators on the line and the elevators continue to operate.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce must be embarrassed by that statement. He knows the Minister of Transport intends to abandon some lines. It must turn his stomach to sit in the cabinet with a minister who so blatantly breaks his campaign promises and so coolly will say to the people in my riding that their rail line must go. I know the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) must be disgusted with that type of dishonesty. Once the Minister of Transport is re-elected he will forget all about his promises. He sets up smokescreens by setting up studies and he teases the people and pretends that their lines will be saved. But when the time comes the lines are not saved. I hope the people who live in the prairie provinces will realize this same Minister of Transport, and his new "Tonto" over there are making promises out of both sides of their mouths.
I submit that our whole transportation system should be pulicly owned and controlled. The prime aims of this system should be to provide a service to the people of Canada, not to make a profit for the shareholders. That should be the prime need to which we should be addressing ourselves.
I say to those in this House who are firm and passionate believers of free enterprise, such as the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan), that there are other areas in which profits can be made. There are other areas in which people can invest their money, rather than investing it in the transportation system to make a profit. If you do, Mr. Speaker, you are shafting your neighbours in the poorer parts of the country. Your are saying that rail lines in Saskatchewan should be abandoned. Small communities in my province would disintegrate because it does not pay to keep the rail lines open to some of these communities.
We should not just look at the ledger sheet. There are social conditions to take into account. If some of these lines do not pay, as long as they serve a good number of people, haul a good amount of grain and other freight, they should be subsidized.
In the future, more and more people may become alienated from the big cities and urban life. There may be more and more energy problems. Perhaps more people will return to the farms and the small communities. Perhaps some day we will have a government that is sensible about industrial strategy
Railway Act
and which tries to help business locate in small communities. If that happens, maybe those communities will grow and perhaps those rail lines will pay for themselves.
They surely will not do that if we take the opposite approach and say the user must pay, that they must be economically viable, that CN must be a commercial corporation and operate like any other corporation. If we take that philosophy, we will all be losers in this country. There will be a few large population centres, but they will not be in Nova Scotia or Saskatchewan. The people are going to congregate in other areas. That is wrong, dead wrong.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate on Bill C-17, another recapitalization of a recapitalized debt of a national railway which has obviously had financial problems right from the start.
It has been most interesting listening to the various comments. Certainly the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) gave a very interesting and entertaining speech. Some of his historical perspective was obviously a little coloured because of his political perspective.
The hon. member said some kind things about me. I would not want to be unkind about him. However, one part of his speech that entertained me was the latter part, when he read off political promises of the 1974 campaign. I don't care if you are a francophone on the north shore or on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, or whether you live in the West in the prairie bowl, in the great sky land or in the Rockies; when you hear that old choo-choo of a train you feel Canadian. As a Conservative, as a member of a party which was responsible for some of these things historically, I agree there are obviously places for state-owned corporations. As the hon. member for Vegreville said in his speech on Tuesday, the then president of the CN, Mr. Donald Gordon, said in a private speech to

That is why I call this the second or third great train robbery. I agree with the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), and especially with the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), that we cannot keep on doing this-in 1952 there was a ten-year plan, and then in 1953 they were getting into debt again-there has to be an end to this somewhere. The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte said we will forgive this time. There is an old song that says "forgive and forget", but I think parliamentarians had better not forget. In 1952, after the debt was recapitalized to the tune of $2.8 billion, the then president of CN, Donald Gordon, entered upon a massive dieselization program almost overnight. Within a year the old steam locomotives were almost all recapitalized. Where is the private enterprise benefactor of all the largesse others have talked about today? subtopic: HEALTH-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO FIGHT CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE
HEALTH-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO FIGHT CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 1, when the traditional heart month was launched, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) what new initiatives she had taken to help Canadians fight cardiovascular disease. What prompted me to ask this question was the statistics concerning the epidemiology of this disease in spite of improved medical and surgical technology. Although a perceptible decrease in mortality from cardiovascular disease has been noted, it is still the number one cause of morbidity and mortality in Canada. In fact, cardiovascular disease accounts for approximately 77,000 deaths in our country. Recent statistics also reveal that there are about 2.5 million Candians suffering from some form of cardiovascular disease.
This kind of incidence is of epidemic proportions, and yet government health authorities do not consider cardiovascular disease to be an epidemic. That is why initiatives at all levels of government are few and inadequate. Cardiovascular disease in our country causes absenteeism, reduced productivity, wage loss, chronic disability and death which in economic terms alone amounts to a loss to Canada which exceeds $200 million annually. Above that, the human tragedy and suffering are incalculable.
Arteriosclerosis is known to be a multifactorial disease with many risk factors, such as obesity, hypertension, tobacco smoking and so on. To date medical research has achieved a great deal to cope with some forms of this disease. But it is clear that coronary heart disease, in particular, has a multifactorial origin. Many factors are related to it in relatively consistent but unknown ways. Many of these factors can be controlled or prevented. Therefore, there is hope to develop a fairly effective preventive approach.
This approach can become more effective if appropriate investigation into these factors is carried out. This means more

research and better public education in cardiovascular disease are needed. In this area, the Canadian Heart Foundation has taken many initiatives and its members and volunteer workers are doing a tremendous job for which they are to be commended. Any increased financial assistance from all levels of government and from the public would be beneficial and appreciated by health workers and especially those people directly or indirectly affected by cardiovascular disease.
It has been well known for many years that most deaths due to acute myocardial infarction, the most common cause of death in Canada, occur within the first two hours of the onset of symptoms and are specifically due to disturbances in cardiac rhythm. Effective electrical and drug treatment of arrhythmias has reduced the hospital mortality, but not the home or community mortality. Therefore, if mortality from acute myocardial infarction and other causes of sudden unexpected death is to be reduced substantially, a major reorganization of emergency medical services is needed. Public education in basic life support procedures, such as cardio-pulmonary resuscitation, is a necessary primary task.
Next, rapid delivery of highly trained ambulance personnel should be available. For this type of case, more public education and trained personnel are necessary. This means more financial resources. But above all, coherent provincial and national policies are necessary.
Therefore, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) can take greater initiatives and allocate more resources to meet this new challenge. A vigorous campaign of federal leadership is urgently needed. The minister could call an early meeting with provincial health ministers and the medical profession to launch a co-ordinated comprehensive program at all government levels to fight this insidious epidemic. Mobilizing all the necessary resources could do a great deal to diminish the incidence of cardiovascular disease.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO FIGHT CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) on his very comprehensive representation. The hon. member is highly regarded as a doctor of medicine and as one who is very concerned about his constituents and Canadians generally.
I am pleased to be able to reply that the government has taken a number of new steps which I hope will help Canadians fight cardiovascular diseases. Several parts of the Department of National Health and Welfare are carrying out activities which we expect will have an impact on the prevention and control of heart attacks, strokes and other problems of the cardiovascular system.
How we live often determines when as well as how we die, and in no condition is the influence of lifestyle more important than in the case of heart attack. Consequently the prevention of premature death as a result of heart attacks is a major goal of the department's expanded efforts to assist Canadians to adopt healthful lifestyles.


On the subject of cigarette smoking, one of the major risk factors for heart attack, I am pleased to inform the hon. member that a series of activities is being developed or is under way as part of a new comprehensive tobacco and health plan. I want to mention especially that the department plans to expand efforts to encourage children to avoid smoking; to focus on smoking by young women among whom, until recently, smoking was increasing rapidly; to review smoking cessation programs and encourage those which are most effective; and to persuade manufacturers to reduce tar, nicotine and other constituents of cigarette smoke.
In a news release on February 2, the minister announced the launching of a nutrition program being carried out by the department in co-operation with provinces, heart foundations and other groups. The program is intended to reduce the impact of cardiovascular disease. Recommendations are designed, among other things, to deal with another of the major risk factors for heart attack, elevated blood fat levels.
I am also pleased to announce that a new departmental publication, "Food and Your Heart", is now available from provincial health departments, local health units and heart foundations.
The newest departmental activity to promote physical fitness is the exercise break package to help fitness leaders and health professionals conduct active breaks for employee groups, elementary and secondary school children and the elderly. Funded by the Federal Labour Intensive Project, the exercise break package will cost some $1.1 million, from a total departmental FLIP allocation of $1.4 million, and will create more that 200 jobs across Canada.
In addition to the above, a working group of Canadian physicians who are experts in the field of high blood pressure are preparing for the department, with the department's cooperation, a therapeutic monograph on this subject. This document will discuss the drugs used in treating high blood pressure and should help physicians in the selection of drugs.
Finally, I want to mention two new developments intended to sharpen the focus of our efforts and to assist in the co-ordination of various departmental activities in the field of cardiovascular disease. The first of these new developments is the establishment of a focal point on lifestyle and health promotion. The main purpose of the focal point is to assist in developing greater collaboration among governments and other agencies in lifestyle and health promotion activities and to bring about better co-ordination of activities within the department. The second development is the establishment of a co-ordinating mechanism for programs concerned with cardiovascular disease within the health protection branch.
Before I close I wish to correct a misprint in Hansard. The minister's reply on February 1 should have stated that the 1978 campaign target for the Quebec Heart Foundation is $1 million, rather than the $6 million recorded.
I have much more to say, but time does not permit. I will provide my hon. colleague with a complete copy of my notes.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-LAY-OFFS IN NICKEL INDUSTRY-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ALLEVIATE
LABOUR CONDITIONS-LAY-OFFS IN NICKEL INDUSTRY-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ALLEVIATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked a question of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) regarding his response to the report and recommendations of the Ontario legislature's select committee looking into the Inco and Falconbridge lay-offs. I pointed out to the minister that the select committee proposed some very practical suggestions, such as a 60-day moratorium on the lay-offs, a 30-day stockpile of nickel, with the two levels of government providing interest-free loans for the stockpiling, a job-sharing program, a retraining program and an improved pension plan which alone would save some 1,000 jobs. I pointed out to the minister that this select committee comprised members of all parties of the Ontario legislature and that in fact the Liberals on the committee all voted for the recommendations without hesitation.
I also pointed out that the committee held a press conference yesterday afternoon at 5 p.m. and released its report and recommendations at that time. However, in answer to my question the minister said he did not know what the recommendations were but that he had requested such information from the Ontario government and was hoping to have the recommendations later on. I asked my question 17 hours after the report was made public. There was a headline story in the Globe and Mail this morning. There were reports on every radio and television broadcast last evening and this morning. The minister rose in the House of Commons this afternoon and said that he has not yet seen the report or the recommendations.
Is this the action and attitude of a concerned minister and of a concerned government? Absolutely not. I have never in all my 40 years seen such callousness and disinterest for people's well-being as I saw displayed, particularly this afternoon, by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). For four months this House has been bombarded with questions about the impending lay-offs at Falconbridge and Inco. A special day of debate was held in this House of the question. Thirty thousand cards of protest were tabled in the House by myself. There were two demonstrations on Parliament Hill by Inco and Falconbridge workers in an attempt to make the government aware of the problems facing these workers.
There were innumerable meetings between ministers of this government, the United Steel Workers of America and the mine mill union. Practically every day for the last four months I have raised the matter in the question period in order to make this government and its minister aware of the problems facing the workers in the Sudbury basin. And for four months, Mr. Speaker, all we have heard in reply is how concerned the minister and this government are about the impending lay-offs. They have stated they were on top of the situation. He was as on top of the situation today, as he was when he heard the night before the official announcement made by Inco of the lay-offs.


Adjournment Debate
What should a concerned minister and a concerned government have done under the present circumstances? Considering the fact that this government and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources have made no positive proposals, upon hearing of the committee's proposal last evening he should have flown this morning to Queen's Park, on the jet the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) uses to travel to and from football games and all the rest of it, and asked to meet with the minister of mines for the province of Ontario. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should have asked to see the report and the recommendations. He should have asked if this problem could be solved by working together.
Even if he had not flown to Toronto, had he forgotten about the telephone system? The House of Commons has all sorts of party lines for members. There is a government Telex system and a member for one of the ridings across the way uses it for his own personal congratulatory messages to constituents. It could have been used in this instance. How callously the Minister of Energy, Mines, and Resources treats the people of Canada when he stands up in the House and brushes off the problem, as he has for the last four months.
He owed this House and the people of Canada, including the workers of the Sudbury basin, a knowledgeable response this afternoon. But, Mr. Speaker, the minister and this government have not displayed a sense of urgency. The lay-offs take effect in four days-Monday. In the Sudbury basin we support the recommendations of the select committee and we demand a positive response from this minister and government. Anything less is a dereliction of duty. This government should resign and let the people deal with them accordingly. I have little respect for them, and the least respect of all for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-LAY-OFFS IN NICKEL INDUSTRY-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ALLEVIATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has just this evening concluded a meeting with Mr. Sidney B. Handleman, MPP, chairman of the Ontario select committee dealing with the Inco Limited and Falconbridge Nickel Mines Limited lay-offs. Mr. Handle-man was accompanied by the hon. Mr. Miller, minister of natural resources for that province, plus other representatives and officials.
The program as proposed by the select committee consists of two components; first, for the first 30 days, the excess production, being that production which would be a direct result of not carrying out the proposed lay-offs, would be financed by interest-free loans provided by the government of Canada and the province of Ontario, as agreed upon by them; and second, for the second 30 days, there would be the implementation by Inco and the United Steelworkers of America of an agreed upon work-sharing program.

The purpose of the 60-day program, according to the select committee report, is to, first, enable Inco to reconsider its early retirement and severance programs and, second, enable Canada and Ontario to develop and introduce a retraining program for Inco workers.
In the meeting previously mentioned it was made clear to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that the Ontario government does not support the recommendation of the select committee regarding stockpiling. Additionally, several members of the select committee submitted dissenting opinions on stockpiling. Indeed, the chairman of the select committee viewed the stockpiling program as counter-productive. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources would also draw to the attention of hon. members that the financing arrangement suggested in the select committee report is in essence a stockpiling program.
The position of the federal government has been stated on several occasions in this House by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and other ministers. On February 8, in this House the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated:
-the department and I have met with senior officers of both the corporations, Inco and Falconbridge, to examine the question of whether or not a stockpiling system would, indeed, assist that industry. Quite clearly, the conclusion of those discussions and that study is that it would increase the problems of the industry, that there is a significant overhang of nickel inventories in this country and elsewhere in the world, and by adding to that overhang we would be delaying the period of adjustment and therefore keeping more people out of work longer than would otherwise be necessary.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources would again draw to the attention of this House that world nickel inventories are at an all time high. At this time Inco's inventory exceeds 340 million pounds and Falconbridge's over 50 million.
Additionally the cutbacks now being implemented by Inco are not sufficient to stop an increase in their stockpile. For example, Inco's stockpile of nickel, even in the face of production cutbacks, will increase during 1978.
The government of Canada strongly supports the concept of work sharing providing the union and Inco agree to the concept and make a joint proposal to the appropriate federal department.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources would also hope that Inco would re-evaluate its early retirement programs and that retraining programs for Inco workers would be utilized.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight pursuant to a question I asked of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) on January 24, 1978. I asked him at that time:
Since the legislation of this government abolishing capital punishment has obviously resulted in an increase in capital murder, particularly the murder of police officers, will the minister immediately bring in legislation amending the


Criminal Code to reinstate capital punishment, which is the ultimate, permanent and effective deterrent to capital crime?
As I expected, the minister answered "No". The first response from the Liberal side of the House was from an unknown member who said:
That is not true; the rate has gone down.
That man does not know what he is talking about. We have lost ten policemen since the infamous incident last year in Moncton, New Brunswick where two policemen were forced to dig their own graves before they were executed by gunfire by their murderers. In less than the past two months we have lost four policemen, in Manitoba, Thunder Bay, New Brunswick and Toronto. The latest brutal crimes are the murder of prison warden Michel Roy in front of his home in Montreal, and also the premeditated capital murder of Miss Healther Zematis by a hold-up gang at the Chalet BBQ on Decarie Boulevard in Montreal. I include this case of capital murder along with the capital murder of policemen and the prison warden because the murder of Miss Zematis was premeditated.
We have got to get back to basics in this country in that any person who arms himself to commit armed robbery is guilty of capital murder if the armed robbery results in a death. Capital punishment was abolished in July 1976 by this House. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the cabinet and the Liberal party made sure it would be, because as the vote neared they scrounged around and organized themselves sufficiently to get a six-vote majority. Yes, they have abolished capital punishment in law, but it is still retained by the underworld and the outlaws of this country. They practice capital punishment upon their victims.
Of all the arguments advanced against capital punishment the most specious and phony is that which pretends to equate the taking of life by judicial execution with the criminal act of a murderer. By the same lunatic logic, then, punitive fines are simply theft and imprisonment is kidnapping. To be consistent, the abolitionists should also want to abolish punitive fines and punitive imprisonment. Indeed, since all forms of punishment are unpleasant actions which it would be criminal for one individual to inflict unjustifiably on another, they should all be ruled inadmissible.
Not all taking of life is murder. The distinction lies in the qualifying word "justifiable". The act of a victim killing in self-defence is not the same as the act of a cold-blooded murderer.
Judicial execution has always been regarded as justified and its justification cannot be swept away by disingenuous logic. To fail to see the distinction between the execution of the criminal and the murder of the victim is simply to be unable to tell right from wrong and is an ingredient in the obscene inequity between our solicitude for the rights of the criminal- though this is indeed a responsibility of society-and our neglect of the needs of the victim, which are nobody's responsibility. The ancient rabbis put it well: "Whoever is kind to the cruel will end up being cruel to be kind."
Adjournment Debate
The expression of society's abhorrence of a crime is an important part of judicial punishment and should not be carelessly disregarded. It is an educational process. Our behaviour may not truly reflect our theoretical test of values but our ethical values will eventually come to reflect the way we act. By treating murderers leniently, our society has learned to take murder for granted and has accepted it as a perfectly natural accompaniment to robbery and organized financial crime. The need for a firm official stand is most urgent. The punishment should fit the crime.
If we fail to recognize these principles, the day is upon us when the recruitment of policemen and prison guards and officials will dry up. Protection of persons and property is the primary, yes, originally the sole reason for government. Without protection for persons and property we lapse into anarchy.
We noted today the answer given by the latest of a long string of solicitors general when the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) asked him a question regarding the murder of Mr. Michel Roy. He said the government was thinking about providing protection for penal officials and guards both on and off duty. Mr. Speaker, we have reached a pretty pass when the government is thinking about hiring security personnel to guard policemen and prison officials in their homes. Guards to guard guards! This is the result of the Trudeau government's betrayal of the people of Canada through lenient and foolish policies which fail tr provide protection to persons and property. This is the result of the abolition of capital punishment, the ultimate permanent and effective deterrent to capital crime. Again, I say: Canada must get back to basics and make the punishment fit the crime.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by reminding the hon. member that the vote on capital punishment in this House was a free vote of individual members of parliament. Let me also say to him that the statistics he quoted this evening are different from those I have seen published. In answer to the hon. member, the ministry is not prepared to accede to a request for the reinstatement of capital punishment in this country. Its position on this issue is well known. However, the Canadian public should be well aware of the concern of the government with the incidence of violent crime in Canada. Significant initiatives in the areas of wire tapping and gun control were the direct result of our concern with the growth of organized crime and the need to control its violent characteristics.
This House has only to look to its present agenda for further evidence of our concern. The relationship of violent crime to the flow of narcotics in this country is undeniable. Our proposals, which would allow law enforcement officials subject to legislative controls to open mails in order to curb the flow of narcotics within Canada, is directed at combating precisely this situation.
In the not too distant future, the next Criminal Code omnibus bill will contain a package of provisions dealing with


Adjournment Debate
increased penalties for the crimes of hostage-taking and extortion, as well as wider powers to deal with the problems of the defilement of children and the distribution of pornographic material which portrays the defilement of children.
It should not be forgotten that in the very legislation whereby this Elouse abolished capital punishment, new rigorous provisions were added to the Criminal Code concerning the eligibility for parole of persons convicted of first and second degree murder. The present law of the land decrees that individuals convicted of first degree murder are to be sentenced to imprisonment for life without eligibility for parole until 25 years of the sentence have been served. With respect to accused persons found guilty of second degree murder, we have now entrusted the jury with the task of recommending to the trial judge whether he should substitute for the ten-year
period which the law would otherwise require the accused to serve before he is eligible to be considered for release on parole, a number of years that is more than ten but less than 25 years.
In summary, the record of this government in responding to the challenges posed by violent crime in Canadian society is, I suggest, unimpeachable. The government is cognizant of the problems posed by violent, organized and serious crimes. It has dealt with and will continue to deal with them in order to best ensure the safety and security of our people.
